article.title: Ice Age
article.author: Unai Montes-Irueste
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Industrial Revolution arrived in a natural world that was still intact. AI is arriving while the climate is already making it harder to meet our most basic needs, and while fossil fuel companies, polluters, and unreliable politicians have already ensured too many people lack equitable access to water, food, shelter, electricity, and healthcare. Add AI and it gets worse. Why keep a call center of workers answering credit-card complaints when a bot can do it? Why hire and train a human being anywhere to do anything an LLM or a swarm of agents can do instead? People will die from this, and not because of bioweapons, the parlor game pundits love. They’ll die because they lose their jobs and don’t survive the loss. The fastest-growing group of unhoused Americans is 55 and older, too young to retire and too old to get hired, and their life expectancy drops accordingly. Some of that will be the price of record corporate profits. That’s the bad news. Here’s the good. Deer survived the Ice Age. So did bears and rabbits. So did enough of our ancestors that we’re here to talk about it. They didn’t make it through on individual brilliance. Related: Southern California Edison Is a Predatory Corporation Getting Rich Off a Basic Human Need Late in the Ice Age, the climate’s long stability broke. Freeze and thaw cycles accelerated, coastlines and food sources shifted twice in a single lifetime, and species built over hundreds of thousands of years for one way of surviving were caught flat-footed. Evolution writes its updates over many generations. When the world changes faster than that, the animals who rely on instinct alone disappear. Humans had something else: brains built to improvise a new behavior and teach it to everyone almost immediately, through language, imitation, and story. One person learns to keep a fire going, and within a generation the whole group knows how. That’s a technology upgrade delivered at the speed of culture rather than genetics. We didn’t out-evolve the Ice Age. We out-learned it. And we did it together. Ice Age bands traveled long distances to trade, find partners, and meet other bands at seasonal gatherings that worked like a regional safety net. If your hunt failed, a neighbor took you in. Hoarding mammoth meat was treated as close to a crime, because everyone eating meant everyone survived the next lean week. None of it ran on genius. It ran on teaching. Archaeologists can trace, layer by layer, an elder beside a child at a flint-knapping site, handing over a cheap stone to practice on, correcting a grip, letting failure turn into skill. Children got scaled-down, working tools. Women ran vast stretches of the infrastructure, from hide processing to waterproof seams to the plant medicine that brought down a fever. Elders were the group’s memory, able to say, this happened forty winters ago, and here’s what we did . When a hunter shattered a leg, the community didn’t discard him. It moved him closer to the fire, where his job became remembering. All of it was stored in story, told aloud, around a fire, by an elder, with the explicit job of keeping everyone alive. The Gwich’in tell of a time when humans and caribou were one being, a story that doubles as law against waste and hoarding. The Inuit tell of Sedna, who withholds the sea’s bounty until the community airs whatever it’s hiding, a mandate for the transparency a winter camp needs to survive itself. Don't gloss over this part. This is the sticking point. Byung-Chul Han draws the distinction. Narrative told around a real fire binds people to one another. What we have now is “storyselling,” narrative repurposed to move product and hold attention. A screen doesn’t gather people. It separates them into an audience of one, at scale. Look around. Kids on Chromebooks in underfunded public schools, and kids at $50,000-a-year private schools, are converging on the same picture: a child and a screen. We swipe to date. We blow through hundreds of Shorts and Reels in a sitting. We watch a show while scrolling a second screen, present for neither. Nothing in real life delivers dopamine at the algorithm’s rate, so real life keeps losing. Related: AI Slop, Collective Amathia, and the Digital Dark Age AI accelerates the trade. It sorts our inbox, which lets us send more email, which makes us need an AI to sort our inbox. It’s productivity inflation, with fewer and fewer humans touching the work as it moves from machine to machine. And because AI runs on a compressed copy of what we already made, it’s a photocopy of a photocopy. Errors get duplicated until they outnumber the truth, and the copy becomes the canon. Meanwhile, our hunger to be together has been identified and monetized. During COVID we were desperate to gather, and the moment everything reopened, the price of gathering went up: ballgames, movies, World Cup tickets. Even the humblest gathering is eroding. Thanksgiving tables are getting smaller, because the person who hosted has died, or the plane ticket, the turkey, and the fixings cost more than one person can absorb. Nobody Zelles each other for Thanksgiving. If the host can’t afford it, there’s no meal. The version of the future the tech billionaires are selling features AI actors eating AI food and having AI conversations, while we sit quietly, dangerously lonely in the real world. It’s worse than the Matrix, where at least you can take a pill and find the world outside the machine. In their vision, there is no outside. Their longtermism, with its Mars colonies, private enclaves, and digital successors, excuses present-day neglect of public health, housing, and climate. It treats the current human era as a stepping stone and justifies underinvesting in the institutions that actually hold us together. And the whole glowing architecture will eventually go dark. A cyberattack or catastrophic outage will take down schools, businesses, and every feed that owns your attention. When no one can remember a phone number, and the old wisdom has been scanned and shredded in the name of efficiency, imagine where we'll be. So what do we do? The answer is written into us. When young people engage with elders and ask, "Why not?" The question is answered. Utopian thinking must be recognized as both the fire we gather around and a discipline rather than dismissed as naïveté We must imagine the place we actually want to reach and build toward it, instead of waiting for catastrophe to force us there. We are not short on wealth, talent, or renewable resources. We can thrive if we put community above productivity inflation and AI saturation. If we can admit that the privatization of public knowledge was a choice, then what was chosen can be unchosen. Related: From El Paso to ICE: When Anti-Immigrant Hate Becomes Government Policy This starts with our schools, which need to return to the fire. Kids from K-12 through college need elders, not AI pretending to be one. They need to apprentice the way an Ice Age child did: practicing and failing under supervision, corrected by a human hand. This also means treating teachers like professionals capable of creating their own lesson plans, and customizing curricula. No more scripted classrooms. No more teaching to the test. Kids need to read whole books. And those who are struggling to read need IEP teams who can meet that child's needs, not force feed them cookie cutter, vendor provided, AI-slop. A bot has no stake in a child's well-being. But we do. We still have, for now, elders who remember the world before the algorithm and the search bar, who found a book with a card catalog because that was the only way. That’s not nostalgia. It’s a living archive of judgment that wasn’t outsourced to a machine, and it vanishes the day the last person who holds it does. We should be apprenticing children to those elders on purpose, right now. Stopping the data centers and breaking up the tech companies is the first step. The next step is reinvesting in an analog world. California just passed a bill to bring local newspapers back to life. Hire young people to work for them. We have a shortage of people who are paid good wages to help those forced into homelessness. Change that. Elders need care. Children need care. Plenty of places need cleaning. Plenty of homes need fixing and building. Pay young people to do all of this work, and more. We must make permanent what we already proved possible during the COVID-19 pandemic: direct cash assistance, rent forgiveness, eviction moratoriums, and debit cards so kids could eat. We need more libraries and librarians, and professionals supporting the success of children and youth who work with families rather than around them. We know we need to guarantee the basic needs and human rights of housing and healthcare, supported by people whose well-paid jobs are to get and keep others housed and healthy, and neighborhoods stitched together with libraries, transit, and business corridors, not carbon copies of corporate retail storefronts and fast food franchises. There's no such thing as community if there's no corner store. There's no such thing as Main Street without a mom and pop shop. We are ecosystem creatures, human and natural, and we have to invest in both. No more cities full of waste. No more beaches with private entrances. No more threats to our water — in Flint or from fracking, in runoff from factory farms, or from plastics and PFAS. No more private land ownership of countless acres by British or Saudi royals, or ranch owners, mine owners, churches, corporations, or billionaires. By saying "No!" to the handful of companies that want to insert AI into everything so that every student, worker, and retired person must accept and use it, we give ourselves permission to say "No!" to every form of hoarding everywhere. Related: AI Is the New Plastic Let’s flip the switch. Let’s pick human beings. What we’ll find, if we try it, is that we innovate more and build things that last when we’re motivated by collaboration instead of competition — when not everything is a race to file a patent, especially since LLMs proved that individual copyrights are meaningless to tech-bro corporations backed by world governments and unscrupulous billionaires. Collective. Collaborative. Shared. That’s what we need in K-12 and in higher education. That’s what we should want for the future of work, in the private, nonprofit, and public sectors alike. What actually got humanity through the Ice Age wasn’t a smarter individual. It was a culture organized, on purpose, around valuing community over the individual — one that elevated the people, women and elders especially, who did the quiet, essential work of holding the group together and passing its knowledge on, hand to hand, around the fire where folks came together to break bread and share stories, not through a device. We’re still here because our ancestors chose each other. That hasn’t stopped being the answer.
